claim: A normal map (or any texture map that encodes raw numerical/vector data rather than perceptual color -- roughness, metallic, height) must have its Image Texture node's Color Space set to Non-Color, not the default sRGB, before being wired into the shader -- sRGB applies a display gamma curve intended for color that would distort the map's actual numeric/vector values. A normal map specifically also needs its color output routed through a Vector -> Normal Map node (not plugged directly into a color input) to correctly decode its RGB channels into tangent-space surface perturbations before reaching the Principled BSDF's Normal input.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched the later chapters of the full video): at 134:20-136:50, an Image Texture node with a normal map has its Color Space switched from sRGB to Non-Color, then its output is wired through a Vector -> Normal Map node into the Principled BSDF's Normal input.
rejected_alternative: Leaving a data texture (normal, roughness, metallic) at the default sRGB color space, or plugging a normal map's color output directly into a shader input without a Normal Map decode node
reason: sRGB's gamma curve is meant for perceptual color and silently distorts non-color numeric data (roughness values, normal vectors) if left on by mistake; a normal map's RGB channels also require explicit tangent-space decoding, not a direct color-to-input connection, to read correctly as surface perturbation.

claim: Rather than editing a source texture image file in external image-editing software, non-destructive in-shader color grading (RGB Curves for contrast/tonal range, Hue/Saturation for color intensity) can be inserted inline between a Base Color Image Texture node and the Principled BSDF, letting the same underlying texture map be reused across variations (weathered, wet, bleached, stylized) by adjusting shader-graph parameters rather than maintaining separate baked image files per variation.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 178:15-180:35, RGB Curves and Hue Saturation Value nodes are inserted between a Base Color Image Texture and the Principled BSDF, drawing an S-curve for contrast and dialing down saturation to remove an unwanted tint.
rejected_alternative: Re-exporting or hand-editing a separate baked texture image file for every color/tone variation of a material
reason: In-shader grading keeps one texture file reusable across variations by parameterizing the look adjustment in the node graph, rather than multiplying the number of stored image files needed for each variant.

claim: For UV unwrapping a curved/cylindrical extruded appendage (a mug handle, a pipe, a limb), place seams along occluded or natural boundary lines (edge loops at handle intersections, the back/underside of the form) so the resulting seam is hidden from typical viewing angles, then use the Gridify tool on the unrolled cylindrical UV island to relax/square it into a clean rectangular grid, eliminating the texture shear and stretching that a raw cylindrical unwrap otherwise leaves along the curve.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 158:40-161:15 and 168:15-169:25, seams are marked along the mug handle's intersection edge loops and the underside, then the Gridify tool straightens the resulting skewed cylindrical UV island into a clean rectangular grid.
rejected_alternative: Leaving a cylindrical UV island unrelaxed after unwrapping, accepting the shear/stretching a raw unwrap produces along the curve
reason: A raw cylindrical unwrap distorts texture lines along the curve's length; Gridify specifically corrects this shear for extruded/cylindrical forms, and hidden-boundary seam placement keeps the resulting cut invisible at normal viewing angles.

claim: A vertex group painted in Weight Paint mode (values 0.0-1.0 across the mesh surface) can be assigned to a Geometry Nodes scatter modifier's Distribution Mask input, acting as a per-point density multiplier that restricts or biases where procedural instances (sprinkles, grass, debris, fur) are placed -- rather than the scatter distributing uniformly across the whole surface regardless of where instances should actually appear.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 202:45-207:40, a vertex group is painted (Front Faces Only) across the top of an icing mesh, then assigned to the Distribution Mask slot of a Scatter on Surface Geometry Nodes modifier to restrict sprinkles to the top surface only.
rejected_alternative: Using a Geometry Nodes scatter with no distribution mask, relying only on face-selection or density-uniform placement across the whole surface
reason: A painted vertex-group mask gives continuous, artist-controllable density variation (not just a hard on/off selection), which a uniform unmasked scatter can't reproduce -- needed whenever instance density should read as intentional (concentrated somewhere, sparse elsewhere) rather than random-uniform.

claim: To give each instance in a Geometry Nodes scatter a randomized but discrete (not continuously blended) appearance from a shared single material -- e.g. varied but flat sprinkle colors, not a smooth color gradient -- route an Object Info node's Random output into a Color Ramp node's Fac input with the Color Ramp's interpolation set to Constant (not the default smooth interpolation) and multiple discrete color stops added along it. This produces per-instance attribute-driven variation from one shared material/mesh, without needing a separate material or duplicated mesh per color variant.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 215:50-220:10, an Object Info node's Random output feeds a Color Ramp's Fac input set to Constant interpolation with several discrete color swatches, assigning randomized uniform colors to each scattered sprinkle instance from one shared material.
rejected_alternative: Creating a separate material or duplicate mesh for each color variant needed among scattered instances
reason: Per-instance random attribute sampling into a Constant-interpolation Color Ramp gets discrete per-instance variation from a single shared material, avoiding the material/mesh multiplication that manually authoring each variant would require -- directly applicable to any large instanced population needing varied-but-not-blended appearance.

claim: A light source's Radius parameter directly controls shadow softness -- a small radius produces sharp, hard-edged shadows (a hard key light), while an enlarged radius produces soft, diffuse shadow penumbras simulating broad atmospheric fill (skylight). Combining a small-radius warm-toned Sun/key light with a large-radius, cool-tinted, high-elevation fill light establishes the classic warm-key/cool-fill color and hardness contrast used in three-point and environmental lighting; enabling Depth of Field on the camera with the focus point set on the main subject additionally establishes optical focal hierarchy by softly blurring the background.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 236:20-239:25 and 248:10-250:35, a warm directional Sun lamp is paired with a cool-tinted, high-elevation Point Light with an enlarged Radius parameter producing soft diffuse shadow penumbras, and Camera Depth of Field is enabled with the eyedropper targeting the main subject.
rejected_alternative: Using default/small radius on all light sources regardless of whether a hard key or soft fill role is intended, or omitting Depth of Field entirely
reason: Shadow softness (driven by emitter radius) and color-temperature contrast (warm key vs cool fill) are two of the primary controllable variables that establish believable, hierarchical lighting in any renderer, and Depth of Field is the equivalent optical tool for establishing which subject the composition draws focus to.
